When Everyday Life Feels Heavy, Exhausting, or Hard to Switch Off

Perhaps your mind rarely slows down, replaying conversations, anticipating what could go wrong, or carrying a constant undercurrent of tension.

At the same time, you may feel flat, unmotivated, or emotionally drained. Tasks that used to feel straightforward, answering messages, keeping up at work, maintaining routines, or staying connected with people you care about, can suddenly feel overwhelming.

You might tell yourself to "just push through", "stop overthinking", or "get back on track", only to feel more frustrated when willpower alone does not shift how you feel.

Anxiety and depression often appear together, quietly affecting your energy, sleep, concentration, confidence, and sense of enjoyment in everyday life.

If these experiences feel familiar, you do not have to carry them on your own.

With the right support, it is possible to understand what is driving these patterns and explore practical, sustainable ways forward.

Could This Be What You're Experiencing?

Anxiety and depression look different from person to person. Some adults experience noticeable worry, restlessness, or physical tension, while others feel weighed down by persistent fatigue, numbness, or self-criticism, and many experience a mix of both.

You may notice that you:

  • feel persistently worried, on edge, or unable to relax
  • experience racing thoughts, overthinking, or difficulty making everyday decisions
  • feel persistently flat, sad, empty, or disconnected from things you normally enjoy
  • wake up feeling tired or experience ongoing changes in sleep or appetite
  • struggle to concentrate, stay organised, or keep up with work and daily responsibilities
  • notice physical signs of stress such as muscle tension, tightness in the chest, headaches, or restlessness
  • withdraw from social plans, messages, or conversations because they feel like too much effort
  • feel easily overwhelmed, irritable, or unusually tearful
  • carry strong feelings of guilt, self-doubt, or feeling as though you are falling behind

Experiencing some of these signs does not automatically mean you have a diagnosed condition. Similar difficulties can arise from prolonged stress, burnout, grief, life transitions, health concerns, or trauma.

A supportive, clinically informed consultation can help clarify what may be contributing to how you are feeling and what type of support may be appropriate.

You May Be Looking for Support Because...

Every adult reaches out for support at a different point.

You may be seeking help because:

  • persistent worry or low mood has been affecting your daily life for weeks or months
  • you feel exhausted from trying to manage everything on your own
  • work, study, or everyday responsibilities are becoming harder to sustain
  • you are noticing changes in your sleep, energy, or motivation
  • anxiety or low mood is affecting your relationships, communication, or confidence
  • you are navigating a major life change, loss, or ongoing period of pressure
  • you have spoken with your GP about a Mental Health Treatment Plan and want to find the right practitioner
  • you want practical, evidence-based strategies tailored to your circumstances

You do not need to have everything figured out before reaching out.

Understanding Anxiety & Depression

Why Worry and Low Mood Often Overlap

Although anxiety and depression are distinct experiences, they frequently occur side by side.

Anxiety tends to pull attention forward, keeping the mind and nervous system on high alert for potential threats, mistakes, or uncertainty. Over time, living in that constant state of vigilance can leave you emotionally and physically depleted.

Depression, by contrast, often turns energy inward, bringing heaviness, low motivation, harsh self-judgment, and a reduced capacity to feel pleasure or hope.

When both are present, it can feel like having one foot on the accelerator and the other on the brake: feeling wired and worried on the inside, yet too exhausted to take action.

Understanding how these patterns interact helps move away from self-blame and toward targeted, compassionate support.

When Anxiety and Depression Affect Everyday Life

Anxiety and depression can influence several areas of adult life at once.

Thinking and Concentration

Persistent worry, rumination, or mental fog can make it harder to focus, retain information, prioritise tasks, or make decisions with confidence.

Energy and Sleep

Difficulty falling asleep, waking during the night, or sleeping longer without feeling rested can leave you starting each day already depleted.

Emotional Regulation

You may feel constantly on edge, easily overwhelmed by minor setbacks, unusually irritable, or emotionally numb and detached.

Motivation and Everyday Routines

Everyday tasks, such as household chores, exercise, errands, or work projects, can feel disproportionately heavy, leading to avoidance and a cycle of guilt.

Physical Wellbeing

Ongoing stress and low mood often show up in the body through headaches, digestive discomfort, muscle tension, shallow breathing, or persistent fatigue.

Not everyone experiences all of these areas in the same way, and symptoms can fluctuate over time.

When Anxiety and Depression Affect Relationships

How Internal Struggles Ripple Outward

When you are navigating anxiety or depression, the impact often extends beyond your own thoughts into your closest relationships.

You might find yourself pulling back to conserve energy, worrying excessively about letting others down, or feeling misunderstood by people around you.

Over time, this can contribute to:

  • withdrawing from friends, family, or social activities
  • difficulty communicating what you need or explaining how you feel
  • increased irritability, tension, or misunderstandings with a partner or family members
  • feeling guilty about not being as present or engaged as you want to be
  • avoiding conversations, conflict, or new opportunities

Recognising these patterns is not about blame: it is an opportunity to explore healthier communication and support around you.

You Don't Have to Figure It Out Alone

Supportive, Evidence-Based Care Tailored to You

Working through anxiety and depression is rarely about "thinking positively" or forcing yourself to feel differently overnight.

Therapy offers a safe, structured, and non-judgmental space to explore what has been weighing on you and build practical tools that fit your life.

Depending on your needs and goals, therapy may focus on:

  • understanding the patterns and triggers maintaining anxiety or low mood
  • developing practical strategies to manage worry, overthinking, and self-criticism
  • strengthening emotional regulation and nervous system recovery
  • rebuilding realistic routines, energy, and gentle momentum
  • improving boundaries, communication, and connection in relationships
  • processing underlying stressors, life transitions, or past experiences
  • building self-compassion and confidence in navigating future challenges

Support is paced collaboratively with you, respecting your readiness and individual circumstances.

What Could Change with the Right Support?

With consistent, tailored psychological support, many adults gradually notice shifts in how they relate to their thoughts, emotions, and daily routines.

Depending on your individual goals and circumstances, therapy may help you:

  • feel less overwhelmed by persistent worry or critical self-talk
  • recognise early signs of stress and respond with grounded coping strategies
  • support steadier energy, sleep habits, and everyday structure
  • make decisions and set boundaries with greater clarity
  • reconnect with activities, values, and relationships that matter to you
  • build confidence in navigating setbacks without spiralling into self-blame

Progress is rarely linear, and a supportive therapeutic relationship can provide steady guidance along the way.

Small Changes Can Make Everyday Life More Manageable

Practical Everyday Steps Alongside Therapy

When energy and focus are low, small, repeatable actions tend to be far more sustainable than major overhauls.

Alongside professional support, many adults find it helpful to:

  • break tasks into smaller, manageable steps rather than waiting to feel fully motivated
  • anchor daily routines around gentle basics such as regular wake times, nourishing meals, and brief movement
  • create a buffer from constant information or screen overload, especially before sleep
  • notice unhelpful thought loops and practise writing worries down rather than carrying them all mentally
  • set realistic, compassionate expectations during high-stress periods
  • stay connected in low-pressure ways with a trusted friend, family member, or health professional

Strategies work best when adapted to your lifestyle, energy levels, and personal preferences.

What Could Support Look Like?

Individualised Care for Adults

There is no single approach that suits every person experiencing anxiety or depression. Your practitioner will work with you to tailor care around your needs, preferences, and goals.

Psychological Therapy

Evidence-based approaches, such as Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT), Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT), Interpersonal Therapy (IPT), mindfulness-based strategies, or psychodynamic therapy, may help you understand unhelpful patterns, build coping skills, and support emotional wellbeing.

Lifestyle and Routine Support

Practical guidance around sleep hygiene, stress pacing, boundaries, and daily habits can complement psychological work and support steadier day-to-day functioning.

GP and Medical Support

Your General Practitioner (GP) can assess physical contributors to fatigue or mood changes, prepare a Mental Health Treatment Plan where eligible, and discuss whether medical review or broader healthcare support may be appropriate alongside psychological care.

You Don't Need to Know Where to Start

Finding the Right Practitioner for You

When you are already feeling flat, anxious, or overwhelmed, researching different therapy styles and practitioners can feel like another exhausting hurdle.

You do not need to have all the answers before contacting us.

At Michelle Barratt Psychology, our team listens carefully to what you have been experiencing, gathers relevant details, and helps guide you toward an appropriate practitioner.

Whether you are:

  • reaching out for psychological support for the first time
  • navigating persistent anxiety, low mood, or burnout
  • holding a GP Mental Health Treatment Plan and looking for the right fit
  • wanting in-person sessions in Brisbane or flexible online appointments

We are here to make taking that first step clearer and more manageable.

Why Clients Choose MBP

Clinically Informed Support, With You at the Centre

Michelle Barratt Psychology & Administration Services (MBP) provides a welcoming, neutral, and professionally managed entry point for adults seeking psychological and allied health care.

Clinically Informed Intake

Thoughtful intake processes help us understand your concerns and identify a suitable support pathway.

Appropriate Practitioner Matching

We connect you with clinical psychologists, general psychologists, social workers, or counsellors whose experience aligns with your needs.

Coordinated Care

Where appropriate and with your consent, practitioners can liaise with your GP and other health professionals involved in your care.

Practical Referral Support

Our team assists with GP referral requirements, Mental Health Treatment Plans, and Medicare-related paperwork where applicable.

Flexible Access

In-person appointments are available at our Brisbane clinics in Toowong and Manly West, alongside secure Online Therapy / Telehealth Australia-wide where clinically appropriate.

You Don't Have to Carry It Alone

You may not be sure whether what you are experiencing is anxiety, depression, burnout, or a combination of stressors.

If everyday life has been feeling heavier than it should and you would like a supportive space to work through it, reaching out can be a helpful first step.

Tell us a little about what has been happening for you, and we will help you explore an appropriate next step.

Contact Michelle Barratt Psychology on (07) 3185 0040 or reach out via our online contact form to learn more about individual and adult therapy support.
